reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Elizabeth got her blue coat from the hook. The zipper was open all the way down. She pulled the pull, but it did not move.

Teacher Sam smiled. "Try the bottom first," he said.

Elizabeth looked at the bottom of her coat. There was a little tooth on one side and a slot on the other side. She pushed the tooth into the slot. Click.

She held the slot with one hand. She pulled the pull with her other hand. Zip! The zipper went up, up, up. The coat closed all by itself.

Elizabeth laughed. She pulled the zipper down fast. Then she did it again. Tooth in, slot held, pull up. Zip!

Teacher Sam clapped. "Your coat is on, Elizabeth."

Elizabeth patted her zipped coat. "All by me," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Madelyn woke up in her warm bed. The sun was on her window. "Time to get dressed," said Mom. Madelyn picked her own socks. One sock was red. One sock was wild with spots. She pulled them on all by herself.

Then Madelyn smelled something good. Mom was cooking eggs at the stove. Mom did the hot part. Madelyn carried the spoons to the table. She ate her eggs and a big apple. Crunch, crunch. When she ate the apple, her tummy felt happy.

After breakfast, Madelyn ran outside. She got mud on her feet. Now her feet were brown! "Bath time," said Mom. Mom filled the tub. Madelyn splashed and washed the mud away. The water turned brown, and then Madelyn turned clean. She rubbed her eyes and yawned. "Sleepy?" Mom asked. Madelyn found her bear. She snuggled into bed. "I wish the mud would come back tomorrow," she whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Henri ran up the steps to Grandpa's house. Today the new baby was coming! Henri wanted to make the baby laugh. He had a plan.

The baby arrived in a soft blue blanket. His name was Sam. Sam looked tiny. Then Sam began to cry. Henri froze. His plan felt gone.

Henri grabbed his fuzzy bear. He made the bear dance. Sam kept crying. Henri found a shiny rattle. He shook it fast. Sam stopped! Sam looked at the rattle. Then Sam made a small gurgle. It almost sounded like a laugh.

"Again!" said Henri. He shook the rattle. Sam gurgled again. Henri clapped his hands.

Grandpa laughed too. "Sam likes your rattle," he said.

Henri followed Grandpa to the porch. "Can I hold Sam now?" he asked.

Grandpa sat down and put Sam in Henri's arms. Sam grabbed Henri's finger and held on tight.

"Hello, Sam," said Henri. "I am your big brother."

Outside, a little worm wiggled on the step. Sam's eyes followed it all the way.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Mateo sat at the little red table. He wanted to paint a picture of his baby sister. But he did not know how to start.

Miss Ana handed him a cup of purple paint. "Try shapes," she said. Mateo dipped his brush. He made a circle. Round and round it went. "That is her head," he said.

Then he painted a square below the circle. It had four flat sides. "That is her body!" He laughed. He painted two small circles for hands. He poured a little more purple paint into his cup. The paint made a soft plop sound.

Next he wanted to make her hat. He tried a rectangle, but it looked wrong. The top was too pointy. Miss Ana leaned over. "Look," she said. "It has three sides."

"A triangle!" said Mateo. The pointy hat sat on the circle head. Just right.

A boy next to him dropped his brush on the floor. Mateo picked it up and gave it back. "Thank you," said the boy.

Miss Ana hung the purple baby picture on the wall. "My turn to look," said Mateo, and he stood back to see.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Paisley's baby doll was crying. It was only a pretend cry, but it sounded very sad. "Waa, waa," said her friend Mia, making the doll's voice. Paisley wanted to help the baby feel better.

She looked around the pretend house corner. There was a small pot. There was a soft blanket. There was a toy spoon. First Paisley wrapped the baby in the blanket. The crying kept going. Then she patted the baby's back, gently, gently. The crying got smaller. Then she rocked the baby in her arms. "Shh, shh," said Paisley. The baby went to sleep.

"Let's make the baby soup," said Mia. They dug in the sandbox for pretend carrots. They drove a toy truck down a pretend road to bring them home. The soup smelled stinky, so they stirred in pretend flowers too. The baby woke up and smiled. "More soup!" said Paisley, holding out the little pot.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Harrison stood at the bus stop with Mama. He held his yellow hat on his head. The sun came out first. The sun made his nose feel warm. "Mama, why do I squint?" he asked. "The sun is bright," said Mama. She put sunglasses on him.

Then the wind blew. The wind took his hat right off! The hat flew up, up, up. "Come back, hat!" said Harrison. Mama reached out her hand. She caught the hat in the air. She put it back on his head. "Wind likes to blow hats," she said.

Next, rain began to fall. Pit, pat, pit, pat. A drop landed on Harrison's toe. "Mama, my toe is wet!" he said. Mama opened a big umbrella. The rain tapped on top of it. The drops could not reach his toe now.

At last the rain stopped. Little white flakes came down instead. "What is that?" asked Harrison. "Snow," said Mama. She zipped his coat up to his chin. Snow landed on his mittens. It did not land on his hands. Harrison looked at his sweet mittens and smiled. The bus came, and they climbed on together.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Henri sat in the big waiting chair. He held his doll tight. Today he would get his first haircut. He did not want snippy scissors near his doll.

The hairdresser waved him over. "Bring your doll," she said. "She can sit on the lap of the chair."

Henri sat down slowly. He put the doll on his knees. The hairdresser put a soft cape on Henri. Then she sprayed water on his hair.

"Look," she said. She sprayed a tiny bit of water on the doll's hair too. The doll's hair went dark and flat.

"Now she looks silly," said Henri. He laughed a small laugh. The wet hair stuck to her head like little stripes.

The hairdresser cut Henri's hair bit by bit. Henri did not move. He watched the bits fall. They landed on the cape like tiny snow.

At last she took the cape off. She shook it, and all the hair bits spilled to the floor.

Henri picked up his doll. Her hair was dry now. It was soft and fluffy again. Henri patted it smooth. "You look pretty," he whispered to the doll.

He jumped off the chair and ran to Mama with the doll held up high.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Leah was three today. She wore her yellow party dress. The backyard had balloons on the fence. Grandma put a big cake on the table.

Leah wanted to blow out the candles. But she was too far away. "Come near, Leah," said Daddy. Leah hopped close on one foot. Then she stood by the cake.

Daddy lit the candles with a match. The flames went up. Leah took a big breath. She blew hard. The candles went out. The smoke curled up into the air. "I did it!" said Leah. Everyone clapped. Grandma cut the cake. Leah got the first big piece, with pink frosting on top.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Beatrice went to the store with her dad. She wanted a warm bun for breakfast. The store was big. Beatrice was small.

She pushed the cart. First it went fast. Then it went slow. "Why does it go slow?" she asked. Dad pointed at the floor. A bump made the cart slow down. Beatrice pushed again. Smooth floor made it go fast.

Next they came to the cold fridge. Beatrice touched the glass. Brrr! Cold glass made her fingers hurt a little. Dad opened the bakery case. Warm air came out. The buns were hot, so Dad used a big paper bag to hold one. Beatrice watched. Would the bag get hot too? Yes! The warm bun made the bag warm.

Dad put the little bun in the cart. "One warm bun," he said. Beatrice smiled. "That is my answer," she said. "A silly bump, a cold fridge, and a hot bun!" She carried the bag all the way home, very slowly.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Sofia wanted to play the senses game at school. But she could not remember them all. "Maybe I can practice at home," she said.

Mama was baking bread in the kitchen. Sofia stood next to her. "Close your eyes," said Mama. "What do you smell?" Sofia sniffed with her nose. "Bread! My nose knows smell!" Then Mama said, "Now look at the oven." Sofia used her eyes to see. "That is seeing!" she said.

Next, Mama tapped the pan. Tink, tink. "My ears hear that," said Sofia. The bread came out. Mama cut one slice. The knife was sharp, so Mama did the cutting. Sofia touched her slice. "Warm and soft. That is my hands touching!" Then she took a bite. "Yum! My tongue tastes it!"

"Four senses," said Sofia. "One more to go." After dinner, Papa took her to the window. The moon was up. "Look how fast the clouds move," said Papa. Sofia looked with her eyes. Then she counted on her fingers. Nose, eyes, ears, hands, tongue. "Five! I did it!"

Papa laughed and gave her a hug. "All five," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Grayson ran to the window at daycare. "Look, look!" he said. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. "Sunny days mean no coats," said his friend Mia. She hung her coat on the hook.

Miss Patel held up a paper sun. "We will make a weather sign," she said. Grayson got the glue. He glued the yellow sun on the poster. It looked bright and warm.

Then the sky changed. The wind blew hard. It was windy now. Papers flew off the table. "Hold them tight!" said Miss Patel. Grayson grabbed the paper hat. He glued it down too. The wind had made the papers fly.

Next came rain. Tap, tap, tap on the window. Grayson glued a paper umbrella on the sign. "Rainy days need boots," said Mia. She showed her red boots. Grayson laughed and clapped.

A shy boy named Sam peeked at the poster. He had never glued before. "You can help," said Grayson. Sam glued on a mitten. "Snowy days need mittens," said Grayson. Sam smiled big. Their weather sign was done. It had sun, wind, rain, and snow. "Let's show everyone!" said Grayson.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Wren sat at the dinner table. She wanted more peas. She reached across the big bowl. The bowl began to tip. "Careful," said Dad. The peas rolled onto the table.

"Sorry, Daddy," said Wren. Dad smiled. He wiped up the peas. Wren looked at her empty plate. She could not reach the bowl. "Daddy, can you help me, please?" she asked. Dad scooped peas onto her plate. "Thank you," said Wren.

Then Grandma came in. She wore a soft winter hat. "My head was cold," she said. "The hat works so well." Wren giggled. Grandma sat down and helped herself. Wren passed her the bread. Grandma said, "Thank you, Wren." Wren grinned and put a pea on her fork. "You're not lazy at supper," said Grandma. "You are a big helper." Wren ate her pea and smiled.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Livia could not find her bunny. Bunny had soft white fur and a pink nose. Livia looked under her pillow. No bunny there. "Where are you, Bunny?" she said.

She looked in her toy box. She looked behind the chair. She peeked under her bed. Bunny was not far away. Livia could feel it. But the room was big, and Bunny was small.

Then Livia saw something move. It was her cat, Milo. Milo tapped a little bell with his paw. The bell rolled across the floor. It went fast, and then it stopped under the blanket. The blanket moved up in a small bump. Livia peeked at the bump. There was her bunny, all cozy and warm!

"Milo, you found Bunny!" said Livia. She hugged Bunny tight. Milo purred and rubbed her leg. "Where are you, Bunny?" Livia said again. But this time she laughed. Bunny was right there, safe in her arms.

Mama came to the door. "Time for milk," she said. Livia carried Bunny to the table. She set out a little cup for herself. She set a small bowl of water on the floor for Milo. Milo drank, and Livia patted his head.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma came to stay for a whole week. On Saturday, Sienna held her hand at the market. "Grandma looks sad," Sienna whispered to Mama. Grandma lived far away, and her cat had stayed home.

The market smelled like bread and flowers. Sienna saw a man with paper and brushes. "Can I paint?" she asked. Mama paid the man, and Sienna sat down. She painted Grandma's cat, black with white paws. "I remember him," Sienna said. She painted his long tail and his little pink nose.

The big clock at the market chimed. It was time to go home. Sienna carried her painting with two hands. At home, she gave it to Grandma. Grandma looked and looked. "My cat," Grandma said. "You made him here with me." She hung the painting by her bed.

All week, Grandma smiled at the painting. When she packed her bag, she folded her clothes around it. "This comes with me," she said. "Then you are with me, even far away." Sienna grinned and waved at the door.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Emilia sat at the big table. Mama put warm toast in front of her. Mama put a little dish of soft butter there too. Emilia wanted to spread the butter all by herself.

Emilia pressed the butter with her spoon. The butter slid off the toast. It fell on the plate. Emilia looked at the spoon. She tried again, slowly. This time she used the flat side of the spoon. She moved it gentle and slow. The butter went smooth across the toast. "Look, Mama," said Emilia. "It is smooth now."

Then Emilia wanted milk in her cup. Papa held the big jug low, near the cup. Emilia poured slowly. The milk went up, up the side. Papa said, "Stop now." Emilia stopped. The milk was at the top, but it did not spill. Emilia looked at her toast and her cup. She took a big bite. An ant walked across the table, far from her plate. "Hello, ant," said Emilia. "I did it myself."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Anthony rode the big bus with Mama. He held his little red dinosaur. Then the bus went bump. The dinosaur jumped out of his hands.

"Oh no," said Anthony. "Where did it go?" He looked down. He looked under his seat. He saw a shoe and a paper. No dinosaur.

The bus went bump again. A paper ball rolled out from under the seat. It rolled right to Anthony's feet. Did the bump make it roll?

Anthony peeked into the hole under the seat. There was his dinosaur! The bump had made it roll there too. It looked like a little nest of lost things.

"Is this your true home?" Anthony asked the dinosaur. "No, you come with me."

He pulled it out. It was dusty. Mama helped him clean it with a tissue. Anthony held it tight all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Florence held Mama's hand on the bus. They were going to the dentist for the first time.

"Will it hurt?" Florence asked.

"First we look at your teeth," said Mama. "The dentist counts them."

A man sat near them. He had a bag with fish and chips. "Do you want to taste one?" he asked his little boy. The boy tasted a chip. Then he smiled.

The bus went round and round. Florence wanted it to stop. She was scared of the dentist.

"Watch," said Mama. She pushed the red button. Ding! The bell rang.

"Did the button make the bell?" asked Florence.

"Push it and see," said Mama.

Florence waited. The man's little boy pushed the button too. Ding! The bus stopped at the next street.

"The button stops the bus," said Florence.

"That's right," said Mama.

They got off near the dentist's door. Inside, a kind lady said, "Open wide." Florence counted her teeth, one by one.

"Ten!" said the lady. "All clean."

Florence picked a sticker. It had a fish on it, shiny and blue.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Leah ran to the swings at the playground. She wanted to swing high like the big kids. But every swing was full.

Leah stood by the fence and watched. Then she heard something. A boy on the bench was singing a counting song. "One, two, three, four, five," he sang. Leah listened. Then she sang too. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!"

A girl on a swing turned her head. She looked at Leah and smiled. "I like that song," she said. "Want my swing next?" The girl jumped off and held the swing for Leah.

Leah sat down and pushed with her legs. The swing went up. She sang her counting song as she flew. "One, two, three," she called to the sky. The girl sat on the bench and clapped.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Arthur was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa had a big dirt patch. "We can plant seeds here," said Grandpa. Arthur jumped up and down.

Arthur made little holes in the dirt. He dropped a seed in each one. Then he covered them up. "Now what?" he asked. "Seeds need water," said Grandpa. Arthur held the watering can. He poured water on the dirt. Splash, splash, splash.

The next morning, Arthur ran outside. The dirt looked the same. "Nothing grew!" he said. "Watch and wait," said Grandpa.

Arthur watched. Days went by. Then one morning, Arthur saw green leaves in the middle of the dirt! "Grandpa, come quick!" he shouted.

The little leaves grew tall. A small yellow flower opened up. Then the flower fell off. Under it was a tiny green bean! Arthur picked it and held it high. "Grandpa! The seed made a bean!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Juliette was so excited. She wanted to give him a surprise. A big red apple would be perfect!

Mommy took Juliette to the market. They walked past the bread stand. They walked past the flower stand. At last they found the fruit stand. But oh no! No red apples. Only green ones.

"Sorry," said the fruit man. "The red apples are gone." Juliette felt sad. Then she saw Grandpa's big straw hat. He was wearing it at the market too! The green apples were hiding under his hat brim. No, wait. They were just sitting in a pile. Juliette had an idea.

"Grandpa loves green apples!" she said. "He eats one every day." Mommy smiled. They bought three green apples. One for Grandpa. One for Mommy. One for Juliette.

At home, Grandpa waved his arms. "My favorite!" he said. He took a big bite. Crunch! Juliette gave him his apple in her own little bowl. Grandpa said it was the best surprise ever.

The next morning, Grandpa wore his hat to breakfast. "Can we go to the market again?" he asked. Juliette jumped up and down. "Yes! Yes! Yes!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Owen ran to the park with his dad. He was so excited. The big slide looked fun today.

Then Owen saw a small dog. The dog was sad. It sat by a tree all alone. "Where is your friend?" Owen wondered.

A loud truck went by. The dog got scared and hid. Owen sat down near the tree. He patted his knees softly. The dog came closer. It sniffed his shoe. Owen laughed. The dog licked his hand. Now the dog looked happy!

Then a big boy ran by and took the dog's ball. The dog got angry. It barked and barked. "Give it back, please," said Owen's dad. The big boy gave the ball back. He threw it far. The dog jumped high to catch it. The ball did not bite the dog's nose. It was soft!

A lady called out, "Buddy! Time to go home!" That was the dog's name. Buddy ran to her, wagging his tail. He was not smelly or sad anymore. He was a happy dog with his ball and his friend.

Owen waved. "Bye, Buddy!" he said. Then he ran to the big slide.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Yesterday, Penelope planted a seed at school. She put it in a little pot. Today she walked over to see it. The pot sat on a low shelf by the window. The top of the soil was still flat and brown. "Nothing yet," said her teacher. "The seed is sleeping. Later it will wake up."

Penelope watered the soil with a small cup. She put the pot back on the low shelf. Then she painted a picture of a green shoot. She gave the picture a tall stem and a round top.

"Now we wait," said her teacher. "Tomorrow we will look again."

All day, Penelope looked at the pot. After story time, she looked again. After snack, once more.

At home time, she walked past the shelf slowly. The soil was still flat. But tomorrow was coming.

Penelope put on her coat. "See you tomorrow, little seed," she whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Jasmine had a library book about a rainbow. She loved the rainbow pictures. At bedtime she wanted to keep the book forever. "Can it stay mine?" she asked. "We borrowed it," said Mama. "We take it back so other kids can read it."

Jasmine held the book close. She opened the front cover first. The words made a story. Mama read them out loud. Jasmine pointed at a page. "What does that say?" she asked. "It says the rainbow is red and blue," said Mama. The words meant something. Jasmine turned page by page, all the way to the back.

Then she got an idea. She would draw her own rainbow book. She drew a red page, then a blue page. "Mine can stay forever," she said. "It's true!" The next day, she gave the library book back. Then she picked a new one to take home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Henry sat at the paint table at school. He had red paint, yellow paint and blue paint. His teacher, Miss Jo, held up a card. "Red," said Henry. "Yellow," said Henry. "Blue," said Henry. "One, two, three colours," said Miss Jo.

Henry wanted to paint a sun. But the orange paint pot was empty. No orange in it at all. Henry looked and looked. He wanted orange so much. His tummy felt tight like a squeezed pillow.

Then Mia dipped her brush in yellow. She put yellow on the paper. Henry dipped his brush in red. He tapped red on top of the yellow spot. He moved his brush round and round. The spot turned orange! Henry gasped. "Look, look!" he said.

He painted a big orange sun. Mia wanted one too. Henry helped her. Red on yellow, round and round. "Orange sun," said Mia. "Two suns," said Henry. They counted them. "One, two." Miss Jo smiled and put a white paper cloud next to the suns. Henry laughed and gave the cloud a tickle of yellow. The cloud turned sunny too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Max saw a big red truck at school. Sam was holding it. Max wanted the truck so much.

Max grabbed for the truck. The truck slipped. It rolled under the pillow corner. Now nobody had the truck.

The teacher, Miss Joy, picked it up. "Sam first," she said. "Then Max." Max sat on a pillow and waited. His sock felt itchy. He wiggled his foot. He kept waiting.

Sam pushed the truck up a ramp. The truck went fast. Sam laughed. Max laughed too.

Then Sam put the truck in Max's hands. "Your turn," said Sam. Max pushed the truck down the ramp. It zoomed right into the block tower. The blocks fell down with a big crash.

Sam clapped. "Again!" he said. Max put out the truck. "You first," said Max.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Riley sat at the little blue table. Teacher Mia put out letter cards. Riley wanted to find the first letter of her name.

She picked up a card. It was M. "M says mmm," said Teacher Mia. Riley put M down. That was not her letter.

Riley picked up another card. It was R. She looked at it for a long time. "R," she said slowly. Then she tried the sound. "Rrr," she said. The card had two little legs and one arm.

Teacher Mia smiled. "Try it again," she said. Riley waited. She looked at the R. "Rrr," she said again. "R is for Riley!"

Then Teacher Mia held up a picture card. It was a rabbit. "Rrr," said Riley. "Rabbit goes rrr!" She laughed and clapped her hands.

Riley put the R card next to the M card. "Mmm," she said. "M is for Mia!" Teacher Mia laughed too.

At dinner that night, Riley looked at her cup. She saw a letter on it. "Rrr," she said. "R is for Riley and for my cup!" Mommy smiled. "Say it one more time," said Mommy. Riley took a big breath. "Rrr," she said, nice and slow.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
David waited by the gate. His tummy made a little rumble. He wanted his snack, and he wanted it now.

Mama came with his bag. She opened it up. Out came his green cup. David drank some water. His tummy felt better. "Snack time at home," said Mama.

At home, David sat at the table. Mama used a safe knife to cut his apple. The apple fell into little white pieces. One cut, and the big apple was small pieces. David ate them all up.

Then Mama ran the bath. The water was warm. Mama checked it with her hand. David took off his socks. He got in the tub. He washed his toes and his nose.

David put on his soft pajamas. He brushed his teeth with Mama. He picked his hat for the morning, his blue one with the star. He put it on the chair.

"Night night, hat," said David. He climbed into bed and closed his eyes.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Sadie sat at the dinner table. She wanted the red jello. But the jello was not ready yet.

"When can I have it?" she asked.

"Later," said Dad. "It has to sit in the fridge. It was wiggly yesterday. It is firm today."

Sadie poked her peas with her spoon. She watched Dad open the fridge. The jello sat there, shiny and red. Now it was just sitting. Later it would be on her plate.

"How long is later?" she asked.

"Later is after dinner," said Mom. "First peas, then carrots, then jello."

Sadie ate one pea. Then two. Then three. She named each bite. "Pea, pea, pea." The peas went down. The carrots went down too.

"Now can we look?" she asked.

Dad opened the fridge again. The jello jiggled just a little. He tipped the bowl. The whole red shape slid out onto a plate. It held its shape!

"Tomorrow," said Mom, "we can make blue jello. Then it will sit in the fridge too."

Sadie clapped her hands. First red, then blue! She ate her jello one happy spoonful at a time.

"What color comes after blue?" she asked.

Mom laughed. "We can talk about it tomorrow."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Charlie sat down at the little red table. Today he would write his name! His teacher, Miss Kim, gave him a fat pencil.

"Pinch it like this," said Miss Kim. She showed him. "Then rest your hand on the paper."

Charlie squeezed the pencil very hard. He wrote a C. It looked wobbly. It wiggled all over like a road with bumps.

"Yucky C," said Charlie.

Miss Kim smiled. "Try a soft pinch."

Charlie lifted his fingers. He pinched soft. He wrote a C again. This C sat straight and neat on the line!

"I did it!" said Charlie.

He wrote the next letter. Then the next. "C, H, A," he said out loud.

Miss Kim clapped. "Keep going!"

Charlie gripped soft, and every letter came out clean. Seven letters, all in a row. He held the paper up high.

"That's my name!" said Charlie.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Jayden was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to build a tower in the yard. He could not find his red blocks.

"Let's look," said Grandpa.

They looked by the blue door. No blocks there. They looked by the yellow chair. No blocks there. "One, two, three places," said Grandpa.

Then Jayden saw something green. The grass by the steps was bumpy. He pushed the green grass aside. There were the red blocks, hiding!

"Bad grass," said Jayden, laughing. "You hid my blocks."

Grandpa smiled. They sat on the porch. Jayden stacked the blocks up high. He put a small blue block on top. Then a small yellow block. The tower stood tall.

Grandpa brought out a plate of apple slices. Jayden ate one, red and shiny. "My tower is the best," he said. He counted it out loud. "One, two, three, four, five!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Amira wanted to sing the counting song. Her big brother Sam knew all the words. Amira knew the first part only. "One, two, three," she sang. Then she stopped. She scratched her head. The rest of the words were hiding from her.

Sam was setting the table for lunch. "Can you bring the cups?" he asked. Amira carried one cup. Then two cups. Then three. "Four, five," said Sam, counting with her. At lunch, Mama put grapes on Amira's plate. "Six, seven, eight," said Mama, counting them out loud. Amira ate one grape. It tasted sweet and new.

After lunch, Papa called from the porch. "Amira, come see!" Ten little ants walked in a line. Papa pointed at each one. "Nine, ten," he said. Amira looked at the ants. The whole little world of them marched on.

That night, Sam began the song. "One, two, three," he sang. Amira took a big breath. "Four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Sam clapped his hands. "You did it!" Amira sang it again, all by herself.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Aurora was grumpy. Her tummy was empty. Dinner was not ready yet.

Mom put a big pot on the stove. Aurora watched from her chair. Mom stirred and stirred. The soup turned red like paint. Soon steam went up, up, up. Aurora sniffed with her nose. Mmm, it smelled like tomatoes.

"It is ready," said Mom. She poured soup into a bowl. The bowl sat in the middle of the table. It was too hot. "Blow on it," said Mom. Aurora puffed with her mouth. She blew and blew. The steam danced away.

Would the soup be cooler now? She touched the bowl with one finger. Warm, not hot! She took a little taste with her tongue. Yum. Then she listened. Slurp, slurp, slurp.

"My mouth heard that!" she said. Mom laughed and poured her some more.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Camille ran onto the ice rink floor. Her dad held a red hoop and a beanbag. "Can I try?" Camille asked. "Yes, you can!" said Dad.

Camille threw the beanbag. It hit the edge. It fell down. "Oh no," said Camille. Dad put the hoop lower. "Try again," he said. Camille threw the beanbag up. The beanbag went in. It sank to the bottom of the hoop. "I did it!" she shouted.

Then Dad brought out a big blue ball. "Catch!" he said. The ball bounced off her hands. It rolled away. "That ball is too big," said Camille. "What do I do?" "Hold out both arms," said Dad. Camille held out both arms. She made a big circle. Dad rolled the ball slowly. The ball came right into her arms. She hugged it like a blanket. "I caught it!" she yelled.

Camille threw the beanbag again. In it went. She caught the ball again. "Watch me, Dad!" she said. Her arms went out wide, and the big blue ball came rolling in.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Jasmine wanted to make the big teddy bear move. She pulled him on the floor. He went slow. Then she pushed the small car. It went fast! "Zoom!" said Jasmine.

Mama came in with warm cocoa. "Careful, it is hot," said Mama. Jasmine touched her own cup of cold water instead. It felt nice. She took a sip. It was a little sour from the lemon. She made a funny face, and Mama laughed.

Jasmine found a string. She tied it to the small car. Now she could pull the car fast. She tied the string to the big teddy bear too. She pulled and pulled. The bear slid across the floor, slow but moving! "You did it," said Mama. Jasmine gave the bear a pat and licked the cocoa foam off her spoon.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Quinn went to the pet store with Dad. She held his hand. There were fish and birds and a bunny. "I want that one," said Quinn. She pointed at the bunny.

The shop lady put the bunny in a box. The box had holes for air. Quinn peeked in. The bunny was very still. "Is it sad?" Quinn asked. "It is scared," said Dad. "It is in a new box."

At home, Quinn put the box on the floor. She opened the top. The bunny did not come out. Quinn reached in her pocket. She pulled out a little carrot. She put it near the hole. Then she sat back and waited.

The bunny sniffed the carrot. Out came one ear. Then out came the whole bunny. It nibbled the carrot in her hand. Dad put water in a bowl. Quinn filled a dish with food. The bunny hopped to the bowl and drank. "You like your new home," Quinn whispered. The bunny's nose went twitch, twitch.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Felix sat in his car seat. The road was bumpy. Bump, bump, bump went the wheels.

"I am hungry," said Felix.

Mom reached into the bag. "Look what I brought," she said. It was an apple. Apples are food. Felix took a big bite. Crunch!

Felix looked out the window. He saw a cow. He saw a sheep. He saw a duck. "Animals!" said Felix. The cow said moo. The sheep said baa. Felix laughed.

Then the car stopped. Dad pointed. "Look, a surprise!" A dog was running by the road. It had a red ball in its mouth. Balls are toys. The dog dropped the ball. It rolled and rolled.

The dog ran after it. The ball went far. The dog went far too. "The ball makes the dog run," said Felix.

"Doggy, come back!" Felix waved. The dog picked up the ball. It came back to the fence. Then it sat.

"Bye bye, doggy," said Felix. He blew a kiss. The dog wagged its tail.

Mom gave Felix a cracker. Crackers are food too. Felix ate it all up.

The car went on. Bump, bump, bump. Felix yawned. He held his apple tight. "Nap time soon," said Dad.

"Night night, animals," said Felix. He closed his eyes.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Alice wants to play on the big swing. But all the swings are full. "How many swings are there?" she asks. Her grandma counts with her. "One, two, three, four." Four swings, and four kids swinging.

Alice waits and counts too. "One, two, three." She counts the clouds going by. Then she hears a boy on the slide. He is counting as he climbs the steps. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" he calls out. Then he slides down, fast, with a little bump at the bottom.

Alice sees the boy leave the swings. Now one swing is free! She runs over and climbs on. Grandma gives her a soft push. "One, two, three," says Alice, pumping her legs. She feels like she is flying, just like in her dream last night. "Higher, Grandma, higher!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Hayden went to the library with his dad. He wanted a book about a cat. He looked on the shelf. One book, two books, three books. No cat book there.

A big book fell off the shelf. It landed on the floor with a thump. "Sorry, book," Hayden said. He picked it up. He could not reach the high shelf to put it back. So he asked the lady at the desk for help. "Can you help me, please?" he said.

She smiled and put the book back. "Thank you," said Hayden. Then she pointed to a small shelf by the window. There sat the cat book, with a cloudy blue cover. Hayden hugged it tight. One book, two books, three books, and one was just right. His dad read it to him by the big window. "The cat says thank you too," said Hayden.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Brooks had a runny nose. He was getting better, but his cough came back at night.

"Mama, my cough is loud," said Brooks.

"We need more cough syrup," said Mama. "Let's go to the pharmacy."

At the pharmacy, Brooks sat in the cart. He saw shelves and shelves of bottles. A man in a white coat waved at him.

Brooks coughed one big cough. The man in the white coat heard it. He walked over and showed Mama a small brown bottle.

"This one helps little coughs," said the man.

Mama put the bottle in the cart. Brooks held his stuffed bear tight.

At home, Mama poured a small spoon of syrup. It tasted like cherry. Brooks swallowed it.

That night, Brooks lay in his bed. He waited for the big cough. It did not come. He coughed one tiny cough, and then no more.

"Mama, listen," said Brooks. "My cough is all sleepy."

Mama smiled in the dark. Brooks hugged his bear and closed his eyes.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Louis stood at the little table. The toast sat on his plate. The butter was soft in its dish.

Louis picked up his knife. He touched the butter. The butter stuck to the knife. Then he touched the toast. The butter stayed on the toast! "Look, Teacher Maya," said Louis. "The butter moved!"

"Spread it slow," said Teacher Maya. Louis spread it slow. The butter went far across the toast. Now the toast was all yellow.

Next came the milk. Louis held the cup with one hand. He poured with the other. A drop chased a drop down the side. "Oops," said Louis.

"Tip the cup less," said Teacher Maya. Louis tipped the cup less. The milk went into the cup. Not one drop fell. "I did it!" said Louis. His heart felt big. He drank his milk and ate his toast. "More toast, please," said Louis.
